performers: Sergei Rachmaninoff, piano; Philadelphia Orchestra; Leopold Stokowski, conductor
question: How does the composer shape the opening when the piano alternates between isolated chords and moving accompaniment?
intro: Rachmaninoff plays the opening of his concerto with Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra on 10 April 1929. This is HMV D.B. 1333, the first 78-rpm side only: its stopping point is not the movement’s ending.

cues.title: One side, not a movement
cues.text: This transfer preserves the concerto’s first 78-rpm side, not a shortened complete movement. Compare the spacing of the opening piano chords with Richter’s recording; the end of this file is a carrier boundary, not Rachmaninoff’s final cadence.
cues.evidence: The HMV label identifies “1st Movement” and “1st Record”; DAHR identifies CVE-48963 as part 1. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800022749
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening gains weight
cues.text: The recorded sound builds across the opening and remains stronger through the following stretch. Follow the longer line as well as the smaller notes: a denser accompaniment need not be the principal melody.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-moderato-rachmaninoff-1929-side1.txt: relative level rises from −22.3 dB at 0:05 to −7.0 at 0:30 and stays around −7 to −8 through 0:45; a novelty boundary occurs at 0:26. This supports the broad recorded contour, not a precise orchestral entrance or comparison of loudness with Richter.

cues.title: Philadelphia, not the publisher’s address
cues.text: DAHR places this session at Philadelphia’s Academy of Music on 10 April 1929. The issued opening is take 3. Camden appears in the catalogue’s publisher imprint, but that address does not establish where Rachmaninoff and Stokowski made the recording.
cues.evidence: The matrix’s take table gives the venue, day and master take; the issue’s MARC imprint is a separate field. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800022749 and https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/173501

cues.title: Pitch can come from the carrier
cues.text: The transfer notes report minor distortion and some wow or pitch warble. Do not attribute every fluctuation to the pianist’s touch: unstable reproduction can bend sustained pitches even when the musicians’ intended notes remain unchanged.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive Technical Notes: “minor distortion; some wow/pitch warble”. This is a source-wide caution, not a claim that a fault begins here. https://archive.org/details/78_concerto-no-2-in-c-minor-op-18-1st-movement-1st-record_sergei-rachmaninoff-and_gbia7026860a

cues.title: A substantial withdrawal
cues.text: The forceful stretch gives way to a much lower recorded level. Follow the continuation through that withdrawal rather than treating it as an ending; the quieter phrases still belong to the concerto’s opening movement.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-moderato-rachmaninoff-1929-side1.txt: the strongest novelty boundary is 2:02; relative level falls from −6.7 dB at 1:55 to −20.6 at 2:05 and −27.3 at 2:20. These are within-file measurements, not calibrated musical dynamics.

cues.title: An American master on HMV
cues.text: This British HMV pressing carries a Victor master. DAHR connects catalogue D.B. 1333 to CVE-48963, take 3; the Archive dates the issue to 1930. A record’s publication date and the performance’s 1929 session date describe different events.
cues.evidence: DAHR lists Gramophone DB-1333 among the issued master’s carriers. The Archive metadata dates the item to 1930; DAHR’s generated MARC imprint gives [1929], so the precise first issue date remains unresolved. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/173501

cues.title: Listen past the format
cues.text: Keep the phrase in mind when this side runs out. The file does not reach the first movement’s final C-minor cadence; comparison with Richter should stay within the corresponding opening passage, not stretch this side across the whole movement.
cues.evidence: The label and DAHR identify this as the first of the movement’s source sides. cache/analysis/rachmaninoff-concerto-2-moderato-rachmaninoff-1929-side1.txt measures the file at 189.6 seconds; its ending is not evidence of the movement’s formal close.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
facts: Moscow Conservatory: piano with Nikolai Zverev and Alexander Siloti; counterpoint with Sergei Taneyev, composition with Anton Arensky

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
